text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Ahmed v. Assu,

2014 BCSC 1768

Date: 20140919

Docket:
S118779

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Mohamed
Ahmed

Plaintiff

And

Sonny
Assu and Lisa Birke

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Fisher

Reasons for Judgment

M. Ahmed:

Self-Represented

Counsel for the Defendants:

M.
Rans

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

September 12,
2014

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

September19,
2014

[
1
]

The plaintiff, Mohamed Ahmed (“Mr. Ahmed”),
claims “monetary relief” against the defendants, Sonny Assu and Lisa Birke, in
the amount of $100,000. He alleges various things, including conspiracy to file
a false lawsuit against him; conspiracy to use a residential rental agreement
to rent commercial premises; fraud, forgery and blackmail; defamation; and
threatening violence.

[
2
]

The defendants apply to have the plaintiff’s claim
dismissed under

Rule 9-5(1)(a), (b) or (d) of the
S
upreme Court Civil Rules,
B.C. Reg.
168/2009 or alternatively that the plaintiff provide security for costs of this
action. They also seek an order under
s. 18
of the
Supreme Court Act,
RSBC
1996, c. 443 preventing the plaintiff from instituting further proceedings
against them without leave of the court.

Notice of Civil Claim

[
3
]

It is difficult to discern the basis for the plaintiff’s
claims as pleaded in the Notice of Civil Claim. It sets out the following
statement of facts:

a.         Defendants
Sonny Assu and Lisa Birke conspired together to file a false lawsuit against
plaintiff Mohamed Ahmed, causing enormous suffering and pain and deteriorating
health of the plaintiff, loss of money, wasting his precious time in court
after returning from abroad, especially during the time of a family death
overseas.

b.         Sonny
Assu and Lisa Birke committed fraud, forgery and black-mail against plaintiff
Mohamed Ahmed.

c.         Lisa
Birke made a secret illegal recording in Plaintiff Mohamed Ahmed’s residence
without his knowledge or permission.

d.         Lisa
Birke and Sonny Assu were conspiring in using a residential rental agreement to
rent commercial premises at 1132 Granville Street, Vancouver, BC V6Z 1L8 for
their business illegally. Defendants did not apply for a business license while
doing business from commercially zoned premises, in which case they defrauded
the City of Vancouver of the City license fees and other requirements and
restrictions, such as they were using hazardous materials and thereby
endangering the other tenants of the building, including and especially
Plaintiff Mohamed Ahmed.

e.         Sonny
Assu through his web log over the world-wide-web defamed Plaintiff Mohamed
Ahmed and used abusive, obscene, degrading and racially motivated language.

f.          Sonny
Assu and Lisa Birke threatened Plaintiff Mohamed Ahmed with violent physical
assaults.

g.         Sonny Assu and
Lisa Birke threatened Plaintiff Mohamed Ahmed with huge financial losses, due
to their friends, supporters and other influence.

[
4
]

The legal basis for the claim is stated as:

Federal Law,
Provincial Law, Municipal Law, Common Law, Abuse of the Elderly and/or whatever
the Court finds applicable or appropriate.

Background

[
5
]

In his submissions to the court, Mr. Ahmed confirmed
that the genesis of his claim stems from a dispute he had with the defendants in
2007 when they were tenants in a building owned by Jutta Ahmed, his wife. In November 2007,
the studio rented by the defendants was damaged from a fire that was alleged to
have occurred in the building. In May 2008, the defendants brought an
action against Mr. and Mrs. Ahmed in the Provincial Court, claiming
damages to their property as a result of the fire.

[
6
]

This lawsuit became protracted. Mr. Ahmed,
representing himself and his wife, denied that a fire occurred in the premises and
he filed a counterclaim in which he alleged that the defendants caused damage
to the studio and were attempting to extort and blackmail him and his wife. After
a three-day trial, the defendants obtained judgment against Mrs. Ahmed and the
counterclaim was dismissed. Notably, the claim against Mr. Ahmed was
dismissed because he did not hold legal title to the property and was not a
party to the rental agreement.

[
7
]

The primary factual dispute was whether there
was a fire. Mr. Ahmed had used a propane torch to repair a pipe in the
basement boiler room, which was located below the defendants’ studio. Mr. Ahmed
had used a fire extinguisher and water hose and the fire department had
attended.

[
8
]

In her reasons for judgment dated July 15,
2010, Dhillon Prov. Ct. J. found that a fire had occurred as a result of
the use of the propane torch by Mr. Ahmed, which was very quickly
contained to the ceiling of the boiler room and the subfloor and floor of the
studio above. She also found that the studio was impacted by the fire by a
pervasive smell of smoke and significant clean-up was required. She concluded
that it was rendered unusable as a studio and there had been a fundamental
breach of the tenancy agreement.

[
9
]

Numerous issues were raised by Mr. and Mrs.
Ahmed both in defence of the claim and in their counterclaim, none of which
were found to give rise to a defence or a claim. One of the issues involved the
allegation that the Claimants (the defendants here) did not hold a valid
business licence during their tenancy (a matter repeated in the Claim here).
Other issues were apparently raised by Mr. Ahmed during the trial,
warranting the following comment from the judge:

[86]      Mr. Ahmed’s
conduct merits special attention. He defended the matter even though he alleged
that the claim against him had been dismissed at the interlocutory stage. His
bellicosity, theatricality, threats of criminal frauds and prosecutions made
towards the Claimants during trial were unnecessary and wholly improper. He was
understandably perturbed about a web log put together by the Claimant Mr. Assu,
the language of which does Mr. Assu no credit. However, Mr. Ahmed’s
remonstrations and protests were excessive. His inability to maintain his
equanimity verged at times on posturing and detracted from decorum in the
courtroom.

[
10
]

Following this decision, Mr. and Mrs. Ahmed
filed an appeal in this Court, which was eventually dismissed in April 2011
due to a failure to comply with orders requiring transcripts to be filed and
security for costs to be paid. They unsuccessfully appealed the dismissal to
the Court of Appeal. There is an unfiled application for leave to appeal to the
Supreme Court of Canada dated December 19, 2011 but it appears that this
was not pursued.

[
11
]

The judgment of Dhillon Prov. Ct. J.
against Mrs. Ahmed required her to pay damages to both Claimants (the
defendants here) in the amount of $3,217.46. On January 19, 2012, a
certificate of costs was issued in the amount of $3,301.60. In June 2012,
a certificate of judgment for the total amount of $6,519.06 was registered
against the title to Mrs. Ahmed’s property.

[
12
]

Subsequently, Mrs. Ahmed filed another action
against the defendant Birke in Provincial Court, claiming $25,000 in damages.
This action was dismissed by Wingham Prov. Ct. J. on December 12,
2013 as having no real prospect of success. It appears that the basis of that
claim was essentially the same as the matter that had been before Dhillon Prov.
Ct. J. I am told that Mrs. Ahmed has filed an appeal of this
dismissal, which is the subject of another application by the defendant Birke.

[
13
]

This action was filed on December 21, 2011.

[
14
]

I will first address the defendants’ primary
application to strike the claim under Rule 9-5(1).

Striking a claim

[
15
]

Rule 9-5(1) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules

provides:

At any stage of a proceeding, the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition
or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no reasonable claim or
defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous
or vexatious,

... or

(d) it is otherwise an abuse of the process
of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
16
]

The test for striking a claim as disclosing no
reasonable claim under

Rule 9-5(1)(a), set out in
Hunt v Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 SCR
959, is whether it is “plain and obvious”, assuming the facts pleaded are true,
that the claim discloses no reasonable cause of action, has no reasonable
prospect of success, or if the action is “certain to fail.” If there is a
chance that the plaintiffs might succeed, then they should not be “driven from
the judgment seat.” No evidence is admissible on an application under Rule
9-5(1)(a).

[
17
]

Under Rule 9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary
or vexatious if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action,
if it does not advance any claim known in law, where it is obvious that an
action cannot succeed, or where it would serve no useful purpose and would be a
waste of the court’s time and public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 2160 (SC). If a
pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, it
may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious. An application under this
sub-rule may be supported by evidence.

[
18
]

Abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(d) is a
flexible doctrine. It allows the court to prevent a
claim from proceeding where to do so would violate principles of judicial
economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of
justice. A claim may be struck where the court process is used for an improper
purpose, such as where a claim is an attempt to re-litigate an issue that has
already been decided:
Toronto (City) v Canadian Union of Public Employees (C.U.P.E.),
Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
;
Babavic v Babowech
,
[1993] BCJ No. 1802 (SC)
.

[
19
]

A plaintiff has an obligation to clearly plead
the facts upon which he relies in making his claim. A material fact is a fact
that is essential in formulating a complete cause of action: see
Young v
Borzoni
,
2007 BCCA 16
at para.
20
. Where a claim is brought by
self-represented plaintiffs, the court should consider whether defective
pleadings can be corrected by way of an amendment. However, it is not the court’s
role to give advice to plaintiffs about how to cure deficiencies in their
pleadings or how to properly present their legal claims: see
Pimentel v
British Columbia
,
[1998] BCJ No. 788 (SC) at para. 20
.

Submissions

[
20
]

The defendants submit that Mr. Ahmed’s
claim should be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a), (b) or (d) on the basis that it is
essentially a repeat of the allegations that were the subject of previous court
proceedings that have been finally concluded. As such, it discloses no
reasonable claim, and it is frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of process
because it is part of a series of repeated lawsuits against them, all stemming
from the same dispute in 2007. Moreover, in each action Mr. Ahmed adds
allegations that judges and others involved in the court process have acted
improperly in carrying out their responsibilities.

[
21
]

Mr. Ahmed submits that he has been abused,
not only by the defendants, but also by a number of judges who have punished
him with costs and sanctions. He says that he is the victim because he was
wrongly sued in the first place and the decisions made by the courts have been
unjustified. He filed an affidavit in response to this application that focuses
on his treatment by several judges of this court as well as counsel for the
defendants. In his oral submission he summarized his claim as involving four issues:
(1) there was no fire; (2) there was a “screw-up”; (3) the defendants cheated
us; and (4) judges acted improperly.

Analysis

[
22
]

In my view, it is plain and obvious that Mr. Ahmed’s
claim must be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d). I am satisfied that the
claim is vexatious and an abuse of process. It is an attempt to re-litigate
matters that have already been considered and any additional allegations stem
from Mr. Ahmed’s view that he was wrongly sued in the first place, the
judgment of Dhillon Prov. Ct. J. was wrong, and the orders of other judges
dismissing his appeal were improper.

[
23
]

The fact that Mr. Ahmed’s appeal from the
judgment of Dhillon Prov. Ct. J. was never heard on its merits is the result of
Mr. Ahmed’s failure to file the necessary transcripts as required for all
appeals. He confirmed that he did not even order transcripts (despite court
orders requiring him to do so within certain time limits) because he did not
think it was worth the $3,000 to $5,000 cost. This proceeding is really a
collateral attack on the judgment against him and another attempt to bring the
same grievance before the court. Mr. Ahmed continues to be upset by what
he perceives to be an injustice against him but he is attempting to use the
court to continue a dispute that has long been concluded.

[
24
]

In addition, the pleading itself is deficient.
The statement of facts contains no material facts to support some of the allegations
against the defendants, particularly fraud, forgery and blackmail. It contains
no proper legal basis for any of the allegations of fact, instead leaving it up
to the court to determine whatever it finds applicable or appropriate. These
deficiencies are so serious that the court is not in a position to consider amendments
to save it.

[
25
]

Accordingly, the claim is struck as vexatious
and an abuse of process. It is not necessary to address the defendants’
alternative application that Mr. Ahmed post security for costs.

Vexatious litigant

[
26
]

Section 18
of the
Supreme Court Act

permits the court to order that a legal proceeding must not be instituted
without leave of the court where it is satisfied that a person “has habitually,
persistently and without reasonable grounds, instituted vexatious legal
proceedings” against the same or different persons in this Court or in the
Provincial Court.

[
27
]

Mr. Ahmed was the plaintiff in
Ahmed v.
Vancouver (City)
,
2012 BCSC 301
. In that case, Sewell J. of this Court made
an order under
s. 18
against Mr. Ahmed. Given that such an order has
already been made, it is unnecessary for me to make another one.

[
28
]

However, I think it useful here to describe
the basis on which this order was made. Sewell J applied the principles
established in
Re Lang Michener et al and Fabian et al
(1987),
1987 CanLII 172 (ON SC)
, 37 DLR (4
th
)
685 (OntHC), which have been followed in many decisions of this Court:

(a)  the bringing of one or more
actions to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of
competent jurisdiction constitutes a vexatious proceeding;

(b)  where it is obvious that an action
cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no
reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief, the action is
vexatious;

(c)  vexatious actions include those
brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of
other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the
assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)  it is a general characteristic of
vexatious proceedings that grounds and issues raised tend to be rolled forward
into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions
brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in
earlier proceedings;

(e)  in determining whether proceedings
are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the matter and not
just whether there was originally a good cause of action;

(f)  the failure of the person
instituting the proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one
factor to be considered in determining whether proceedings are vexatious;

(g)  the
respondent’s conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from judicial
decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal proceedings.

[
29
]

Sewell J found that Mr. Ahmed had not only
sought to re-litigate matters already decided against him but also had a
history of commencing actions that were “manifestly devoid of merit” in which
he typically made serious allegations about the character and motivation of
other parties “without any foundation whatsoever”. At paras. 45 - 52 he
outlined other actions brought by Mr. Ahmed to support his conclusions.
One of those actions was the one before me.

[
30
]

Sewell J’s order under
s. 18
was made after
Mr. Ahmed commenced this proceeding; hence it was not caught under that
order thus necessitating the application to strike.

Costs

[
31
]

Rule 9-5(1) provides that the court may order
the costs of the application to be paid as special costs. The defendants seek
special costs, payable forthwith.

[
32
]

Special costs may be awarded in circumstances
where a litigant’s conduct is reprehensible such that it is worthy of rebuke or
chastisement:
Garcia v Crestbrook Forest Industries Ltd.
(1994),
1994 CanLII 2570 (BC CA)
, 9 BCLR
(3d) 242 (CA). An attempt to re-litigate matters with a reckless indifference
to prior court orders has been held to be reprehensible conduct:
Muller v
Muller
,
2010 BCSC 1381
.

[
33
]

Mr. Ahmed’s claim has been struck as vexatious
and an abuse of process. That in itself does not necessarily result in a
finding of reprehensible conduct. However, Mr. Ahmed has behaved badly in this
matter, making serious allegations against not only the defendants, but also
against their counsel and various judges who have made orders along the way. It
appears to me that he honestly believes he has been wronged but he is not able
to act with reason and accept that this matter was concluded long ago. His
conduct in this litigation and his continued disregard of court orders can only
be described as reprehensible conduct worthy of rebuke, justifying an order for
special costs.

Order

[
34
]

The plaintiff’s claim is struck under Rule
9-5(1)(b) and (d) and the defendants are awarded special costs in this
application.

“Fisher J.”
